BEFORE THE FEDERAL ENERGY REGULATORY COMMISSION


In the Matter of the Application of:)
                                    )
DeepGreen Cook Inlet SPV, LLC       )               Docket No. P-15423-000
DeepGreen Cook Inlet Subsea-Compute )
and Infrastructure Hub Project      )


                                       Defenders of Wildlife
                                        Motion to Intervene

       Pursuant to Rule 214 of the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission's (FERC) Rules

of Practice and Procedure, 18 C.F.R. § 385.214, Defenders of Wildlife (Defenders) moves to

intervene in the above-referenced proceeding regarding the preliminary permit application

of DeepGreen Cook Inlet SPV, LLC (DeepGreen) for the proposed DeepGreen Cook Inlet

Subsea-Compute and Infrastructure Hub Project (project). This motion is filed in response

to the Notice of Preliminary Permit Application Accepted for Filing and Soliciting

Comments, Motions to Intervene, and Competing Applications published in the Federal

Register on September 4, 2026, 91 FR 56879, Docket No. P-15423-000. This filing is timely

as it is submitted before the deadline for intervention established by FERC in its Notice of

Application. Defenders has a direct and substantial interest in this proceeding that no

other party can adequately represent. By moving to intervene to obtain party status,

Defenders seeks to protect its interests in the conservation of the endangered Cook Inlet

beluga whale, the threatened Southwest Alaska distinct population segment of the

northern sea otter, the unique Cook Inlet ecosystem on which these and other wildlife

species depend, and the appropriate interpretation and implementation of our nation’s



                                                1
 flagship wildlife conservation statutes, including the Endangered Species Act and the

Marine Mammal Protection Act.

  I.   Notices and Communications

       Service is to be made upon and communications regarding this proceeding should

be addressed to:

Joseph M. Manning                         Jane P. Davenport
Defenders of Wildlife                     Defenders of Wildlife
1130 17th Street, NW                      1130 17th Street, NW
Washington, DC 20036-4604                 Washington, DC 20036-4604
Phone: 202-866-0073                       Phone: 202-772-3274
Fax: 202-682-1331                         Fax: 202-682-1331
jmanning@defenders.org                    jdavenport@defenders.org

 II.   Proposed Project

       On February 11, 2026, DeepGreen filed an application with the FERC for a

preliminary permit, pursuant to section 4(f) of the Federal Power Act, for a proposed

underwater AI data center. DeepGreen subsequently supplemented its application on June

26, 2026, and on September 1, 2026, FERC accepted the updated application.

       The project would be in the Upper Cook Inlet, East Foreland Corridor, Kenai

Peninsula Borough, Alaska. DeepGreen identifies an approximately 1,400- to 1,650-acre

project area centered in the deep-water Cook Inlet thalweg. The preliminary permit would

preserve DeepGreen’s priority to apply for a license while it conducts environmental,

engineering, and interconnection studies; construction of the project would require further

authorizations.

       The proposed Project includes a 100-megawatt tidal-energy generation facility and

data center. Its principal components would include approximately 330 to 350 marine


                                             2
 hydrokinetic turbines and 66 subsea “hives” (data center pods) with server racks. The

proposal also includes construction of scour skirts and a 3.5-mile subsea cable to connect

the offshore hub to a landing site in the Nikiski Industrial Corridor.

III.   Interest of the Intervenor

       Defenders has interests and represents its members’ interests that will be directly

affected by the outcome of these proceedings. Under FERC’s Rule of Practice and

Procedure 214, a party seeking intervention must state its “interest” in the proceeding by

demonstrating it “has or represents an interest which may be directly affected by the

outcome of the proceedings” or that its “participation is in the public interest.” 18 C.F.R. §

385.214(b)(2).

       Defenders of Wildlife is a 501(c)(3) non-profit corporation headquartered in

Washington, DC, with offices nationwide, including in Alaska. For nearly 80 years,

Defenders has worked to protect and restore America’s wildlife at risk of extinction,

advancing a vision of a future in which wildlife thrives, sustained by broad public support

and a resilient network of healthy lands and waters. Defenders has more than 1.8 million

members and supporters, including more than 4,300 in Alaska. Defenders’ policy, legal,

science, and advocacy experts work at every level to transform policies and craft solutions

for wildlife on behalf of our members.

       For years Defenders has worked to protect Alaskan wildlife, including Cook Inlet

belugas and northern sea otters. For example, Defenders and our partners petitioned to list

the Cook Inlet beluga whale as an endangered species in 2007 and pushed for designation

of over 3,000 square miles of critical habitat in April 2011. Defenders also helped develop


                                                3
 the Cook Inlet Beluga Recovery Plan and serves on the Outreach Committee of the Cook

Inlet Beluga Recovery Task Force. Additionally, Defenders is a partner of the Alaska Beluga

Whale Monitoring Partnership. Defenders works with citizen scientist volunteers to monitor

belugas at multiple locations throughout Cook Inlet. Defenders funded and launched the

Anchorage Coastal Beluga Survey in 2008, and in 2017 helped create the popular annual

‘Belugas Count!’ program to engage and inform local residents about Cook Inlet

belugas. Defenders has also been leading a contaminant study in Cook Inlet for over three

years, evaluating contaminants in the water and prey of both belugas and sea otters. This

project has brought together stakeholders interested in Cook Inlet water quality together by

hosting multiple Cook Inlet Water Quality summits and stakeholder meetings.

       Moreover, Defenders’ members live, work, visit, and recreate in Alaska. Many of our

members visit Cook Inlet to look for, photograph, study, and otherwise enjoy its unique

wildlife, including belugas and sea otters. This project threatens both species.

       First, DeepGreen proposes to build an underwater data center within the critical

habitat of Cook Inlet beluga whales. There are approximately 331 individuals in the

population, and the Marine Mammal Commission cautions that the population’s low

growth rate, combined with increasing human activity in beluga habitat, raise significant

concern about whether it can recover. NMFS, New Abundance Estimate for Endangered

Cook Inlet Beluga Whales, https://www.fisheries.noaa.gov/feature-story/new-abundance-

estimate-endangered-cook-inlet-beluga-whales; Marine Mammal Comm’n, Cook Inlet

Beluga Whale, https://www.mmc.gov/priority-topics/species-of-concern/cook-inlet-

beluga-whale/. NMFS’s 2016 Recovery Plan for the Cook Inlet Belugas identified noise,


                                              4
 habitat loss, and reduction in prey as threats to beluga recovery. National Marine Fisheries

Service, Recovery Plan for the Cook Inlet Beluga Whale, 2016, available at

https://www.fisheries.noaa.gov/resource/document/recovery-plan-cook-inlet-beluga-

whale-delphinapterus-leucas. Unfortunately, the project with up to 350 tidal turbines and

66 server centers is likely to create all three threats by impeding access to the Cook Inlet

Beluga breeding and feeding grounds, contributing to a reduction in prey, and resulting in

noise pollution that threatens beluga survival and recovery.

       Second, Cook Inlet also contains two distinct population segments (DPS) of

northern sea otter—the Southwest Alaska DPS and the Southcentral Alaska DPS. The

Southwest Alaska DPS is listed as threatened under the Endangered Species Act (ESA) and

can be found on the western shore of Cook Inlet. The Southcentral Alaska DPS is protected

by the Marine Mammal Protection Act (MMPA) and can be found on the eastern shore of

Cook Inlet. The project poses a threat to sea otters through increased harassment from

vessel traffic and noise pollution and may alter sea otter habitat in a manner that reduces

prey availability.

       Finally, Defenders has worked for decades to ensure the appropriate interpretation

and implementation of two of our nation’s flagship wildlife conservation statutes, the ESA

and the MMPA, including for both onshore and offshore projects in Alaska. Defenders has a

strong institutional interest in ensuring that federal agencies such as FERC scrupulously

comply with their obligations under these statutes, including the procedural and

substantive obligations of ESA section 7(a)(2), 16 U.S.C. § 1536(a)(2), as well as the

incidental take permitting obligations of both the ESA and the MMPA. These obligations


                                              5
 inhere at the preliminary license phase of a FERC FPA proceeding such as this one where

studies to be carried out under a preliminary license may adversely affect listed species or

designated critical habitat or may result in the incidental take of protected species.

       Defenders and its members will be directly affected by the outcome of these

proceedings. Defenders and its members use and enjoy the waters of Cook Inlet. As

demonstrated through Defenders’ ongoing work to protect Cook Inlet wildlife, Defenders

has a substantial interest in this proceeding and the project’s potential impacts on Cook

Inlet belugas and northern sea otters. Defenders seeks to intervene to protect this interest

and to ensure its members’ and the public’s interest in the proper implementation of the

ESA and MMPA is vindicated.

IV.    Statement of Position

       Under FERC’s Rule of Practice and Procedure 214, a party seeking intervention must

state “to the extent known” its “position” and basis in fact and law for its position. 18 C.F.R.

§ 385.214(b)(1). Defenders opposes the proposed preliminary permit due to concerns

about the potential impacts on Cook Inlet beluga whale and northern sea otters. Defenders

reserves the right to modify this position as more details about the project emerge.

However, based on the information available, Defenders objects to the issuance of a

preliminary permit because of the project impacts described below.1

           A. Impacts to Cook Inlet Beluga Whales




1
 Defenders has also submitted detailed technical comments, which are incorporated here
by reference.
                                               6
        Belugas’ high auditory sensitivity, wide frequency bandwidth, and dependence on

sound to navigate, communicate, and find prey make them vulnerable to noise, which can

mask their signals or, if intense, lead to hearing impairment. National Marine Fisheries

Service, Recovery Plan for the Cook Inlet Beluga Whale, 2016, at Appendix E, p. IX-27. The

project would add noise in every phase: survey and vessel traffic, installation of hundreds

of turbine cradles and a cable landing, and, unlike a conventional construction project,

continuous operational noise from 330 to 350 turbines and 66 compute pods running

around the clock. Notably, even if FERC never grants a license, the preliminary license

alone and the studies conducted pursuant to it will add ocean noise to beluga habitat.

       The preliminary phase of feasibility and environmental planning for this project can

be anticipated to involve on-water work such as hydrographic studies, seismic surveys,

echosounders, and bathymetry, all of which will increase the underwater noise levels of

Cook Inlet and require repeated vessel trips. DeepGreen has demonstrated no awareness

of the potential for these activities to interfere with beluga behavior, nor has it accounted

for how these activities would add to the noise and industrial activity already affecting

Cook Inlet belugas.

       Further, studies conducted under the preliminary license can be anticipated to

involve activities on the seafloor, such as placing and retrieving survey and monitoring

equipment, potentially disturbing this benthic habitat and affecting belugas. Finally, any

survey activities will of necessity involve additional vessel traffic, increasing the risk of

vessel strikes.




                                                7
        The impacts will only be worsened during the construction and operations phases, if

FERC licenses DeepGreen to proceed. Noise from construction could interfere with the

reproductive success and survival of belugas. Id. at Appendix E, p. IX-29. Likewise,

operating 350 turbines and 66 subsea data centers will generate constant noise that could

cloak the sounds belugas rely on to feed, way find and communicate. Chronic sources

raise the background noise level over long periods. Yet DeepGreen offers no source levels,

propagation modeling, or acoustic baseline.

       Beyond noise impacts, Defenders is concerned about both the placement of the

project and the project’s potential impacts on beluga prey. The proposed turbine and data

center array and cable would occupy a corridor that press reports describe as the

narrowest point of the inlet. Alaska fishing and wildlife groups raise alarm over proposal for

underwater Cook Inlet data center, Alaska Journal of Commerce (Oct. 4, 2026). As such,

the project may impede access to the species’ breeding and feeding grounds and

DeepGreen has not shown how “unrestricted passage” for belugas would be preserved.

       Beluga whale prey includes Chinook, sockeye, chum, and coho salmon and

eulachon, which migrate through the project area. Salmon are particularly sensitive to

changes in water temperature. They need cold water to develop their eggs, keep their

metabolism stable and prevent energy depletion during long migratory journeys. The

project, however, will generate a continuous thermal load that must be dissipated into

Cook Inlet through passive cooling. DeepGreen has provided no thermal plume model, no

dispersion analysis, and no heat budget nor has it accounted for how these changes to the

water column may impact these species.


                                              8
            B. Impacts to Northern Sea Otters

       Although sea otters are less dependent on underwater sound to navigate, hunt, or

communicate than other marine species, human-made noise impacts sea otters by

altering their behavior, causing stress, and risking hearing damage. Sea otters in Alaska

exhibit escape behaviors in response to the presence and approach of vessels. 89 Fed.

Reg. 38,167, 38,172 (May 7, 2024). Increased vessel traffic is a foreseeable impact of the

preliminary and construction phases. Additionally, loud noises during construction

activities, such as pile driving, may result in sea otters demonstrating startle responses,

changing direction of travel, diving, or prematurely surfacing. Sea otters reacting to survey

and construction activities may divert time and attention from biologically important

behaviors, such as feeding and nursing pups.

       Sea otters may also be impacted by the noise generated by the ongoing operation of

the project. Sea otters in Cook Inlet have been observed to swim to avoid a close approach

of drilling rigs—despite near-ambient noise levels—when drifting on a tide trajectory that

would have taken them within 500 m (0.3 mi) of an active offshore drilling rig. Id. at 38,172.

Sea otter responses to disturbance can result in energetic costs, which increases the

amount of prey required. This increased prey consumption may impact prey availability

and cause sea otters to spend more time foraging and less time resting.

       Likewise, sea otters in Cook Inlet rely heavily on benthic habitats to forage for

invertebrates like clams, crabs, and sea urchins. The project proposes disruptions

including trenching, scour protection units, and 3.5-miles of subsea cables that could alter

local seafloor structures and prey availability. Id. at 38,173–74.


                                               9
        Finally, sea otters depend on their fur for insulation and are highly vulnerable to oil

and other contaminants. Marine Mammal Comm’n, Northern Sea Otters,

https://mmc.gov/priority-topics/species-of-concern/northern-sea-otters. The application

discloses no measures to prevent releases of fuel, fluids, or other contaminants.

           C. ESA and MMPA Compliance

       It is Defenders’ position that ESA and MMPA compliance is required before FERC

may grant DeepGreen’s application for preliminary license under the FPA.

       The MMPA imposes a moratorium on all unauthorized incidental take. 16 U.S.C. §§

1371, 1372. Incidental take, including take via harassment, may only be authorized under

16 U.S.C. § 1371(a)(5)(A) or (D). Separately, the ESA also prohibits unauthorized incidental

take of endangered and some threatened wildlife species, id. § 1538(a)(1), a prohibition

that extends to any person causing another to commit unauthorized incidental take,

including by issuing permits that are conditions precedent to lawful activities that may

result in incidental take, id. § 1538(g). Notably, incidental take authorization under the

MMPA is a statutory prerequisite to incidental take authorization via an incidental take

statement issued under the ESA for any listed marine mammals. Id. § 1536(b)(4).

       Separately, the ESA obligates FERC to comply with the mandate to ensure any

action it authorizes, funds, or carries out is not likely to jeopardize the continued existence

of any listed species or destroy or adversely modify designated critical habitat. Id. §

1536(a)(2). To comply with this substantive obligation, FERC must consult with NMFS

and/or FWS wherever its action may affect listed species or critical habitat. Unless FWS or




                                              10
 NMFS concurs with FERC’s conclusion that its action may affect but is not likely to

adversely affect a listed species or critical habitat, formal consultation is required.

       Here, it is Defenders’ position that a preliminary license—a statutory condition

precedent to any in-water survey activities by DeepGreen—requires both MMPA

compliance to ensure any incidental take, including harassment, is authorized, and ESA

compliance to ensure against likely jeopardy or the destruction or adverse modification of

designated critical habitat from such survey activities. To fulfill these obligations, FERC

must consult with FWS for northern sea otter and NMFS for Cook Inlet beluga whales.

Further, because MMPA incidental take authorization is a statutory condition precedent to

ESA incidental take authorization for listed marine mammals, FERC must require that

DeepGreen apply for and obtain all necessary MMPA authorizations before it may issue a

preliminary license that results in incidental take of either species.

 V.    Conclusion

       Defenders and its members have worked to protect imperiled species, including

Cook Inlet Belugas and northern sea otters, for nearly 80 years. As such, Defenders has

and represents an interest that is directly affected by the outcome of this proceeding. Only

through intervention will Defenders be able to represent its interest in the protection of

Cook Inlet belugas and northern sea otters and ensure the proper administration of the ESA

and MMPA. Defenders respectfully requests that FERC grant its motion to intervene in this

matter, Docket No. P-15423-000.
